h1:
What to Eat in Phuket
Hokkien · Southern Thai · Fresh Seafood
intro: Phuket is more than beaches and sea — it's a food town with roots you won't find anywhere else. Hokkien cooking brought by Chinese tin-mining families mixed with fiery southern Thai flavours and the island's Peranakan (Baba) heritage to create a cuisine all its own. This guide rounds up the dishes Phuket locals actually eat day to day, with the real spots, the real neighbourhoods and rough prices — so your first meal on the island doesn't go to waste.

blocks.html: Ask a Phuket local what the island's signature dish is, and the answer usually isn't the grilled seafood by the beach that tourists know. It's a hot bowl of Hokkien mee in the morning, dim sum sold before the sun is even up, and sweet-savoury moo hong eaten over steamed rice. The town took in Hokkien-Chinese culture back in the tin-mining days, then slowly blended it with southern Thai flavours into a Peranakan style of cooking you won't taste anywhere else. Here's what we'd send you to try.

blocks.text: Hokkien Mee — One Bowl That Explains Phuket

blocks.html: Hokkien mee is a thick, yellow egg noodle, either stir-fried or blanched in a rich broth with prawns, squid, pork and vegetables, seasoned with black pepper and dried shrimp until it's fragrant. It's a legacy of the Hokkien families who came over during the mining era, with the local kitchens later tuning it to a southern Thai palate. Some places call it mee sapam, after the fishing village that has been making these noodles for generations.

items.name: Mee Ton Poe
items.blurb: The stuff of Phuket Hokkien-mee legend, going since 1946, with a slogan locals still repeat: "come to Phuket, you have to eat Mee Ton Poe." The standout is the stir-fried Hokkien mee, cooked hot and smoky off the wok, topped with a soft-cooked egg and fresh seafood. You eat it under the big bodhi tree out front, the way Phuket folks have for decades.
items.meta: Phuket Road, Old Town · roughly 10:00–18:30 (Tue–Wed until 20:00)

items.name: Ko Yoon
items.blurb: An old-guard noodle shop deep in the Old Town that locals rate as having one of the deepest, most dried-shrimp-fragrant broths around. The noodles have just the right chew, and the setting is a classic old shophouse.

items.name: Mee Sapam
items.blurb: A noodle shop in Sapam village going since 1952 — the original of Hokkien noodles stir-fried with soy and seafood. It's the long-standing spot that turned "mee sapam" into shorthand for Phuket-style Hokkien mee.

blocks.title: Know before you go
blocks.html: Many of the old-guard Hokkien-mee shops close in the afternoon, and some have unpredictable days off. If you're set on a famous one, aim for late morning to midday and check the shop's closing day first — they tend to sell out fast.

blocks.text: Southern Thai and Peranakan — Bold Flavours Phuket Does Well

blocks.html: Beyond noodles, Phuket is a town for fiery southern Thai food and hard-to-find Baba dishes. The one you can't skip is moo hong — pork belly braised with garlic, pepper, soy and palm sugar until it's fall-apart tender, sweet and savoury in equal measure, eaten over steamed rice. Follow it with crab curry with wild betel leaf, shrimp-paste chilli dip with grilled fish, and stink beans stir-fried with fresh prawns for that proper southern heat.

items.name: Tu Kab Khao
items.blurb: A southern Thai and Baba restaurant set in an old building in Phuket Town, with a Michelin nod. It serves moo hong, crab curry and local Phuket dishes in a handsome setting — good for a special meal.

items.name: Kopitiam by Wilai
items.blurb: An old shophouse on Thalang Road, walls lined with photos of old Phuket, serving Hokkien mee, mee hoon and thick, old-style kopi coffee.

items.name: Lock Tien
items.blurb: A 1950s food court on the corner of Dibuk and Yaowarat roads, gathering long-running Peranakan and Hokkien stalls under one roof. Open morning to afternoon, busiest when locals come in for lunch.

blocks.text: Morning Dim Sum — The Phuket Food Worth an Early Start

blocks.html: Dim sum is a serious morning ritual in Phuket. Plenty of shops open from 6am and sell out before mid-morning, and locals like to settle in with dim sum and old-style coffee before the day starts. To catch the real atmosphere, you'll have to be willing to get up early.

items: Boonrat Dim Sum — has been serving traditional Cantonese-recipe dim sum to Phuket since 1917. Open roughly 6:00–10:00; show up late and you risk no seat.
Old-style coffee with your dim sum — order a kopi (black coffee with condensed milk) or a hot pulled tea on the side. It's the standard Old Town breakfast set.
Moo hong and rice porridge — many dim sum shops have moo hong and dressed-up rice porridge to add on for a proper, filling breakfast.

blocks.title: Dim sum tip
blocks.html: The famous dim sum shops in Phuket are mostly cash-only and the queues get long on weekends. If you miss the morning window, look for a dim sum shop that stays open all day around the Old Town instead — it may not match the legends, but it's still good.

blocks.text: Fresh Seafood — Eating Local at Rawai and the Piers

blocks.html: Phuket seafood is at its best eaten close to where it's caught. The spots locals go to are the Rawai fishing village on the south of the island and the pier-side restaurants on the east coast. Here the prawns, crab, squid and fish come straight off the fishing boats, priced by weight and quite a bit cheaper than the tourist beach zones.

items.name: Rawai Seafood Market
items.blurb: Phuket's long-established fishing village, where you pick fresh seafood from the stalls by weight, then walk it to one of the shops next door to cook for you. You eat it fresh and support the local fishing community directly. It's on the dirt road to the left, just before Rawai pier.

items.name: Laem Hin Seafood
items.blurb: A restaurant at the end of Laem Hin pier on the east coast, with seafood kept live in pens that you can see for yourself. Bold Thai flavours, fair prices, and views over the water and the little islands offshore.
items.meta: Laem Hin, east coast · open daily 10:00–21:00

items.name: Kan Eang @ Pier
items.blurb: One of Phuket's veteran seafood spots — the original opened in 1973, about 50 years ago — set on Chalong Bay beside Chalong pier and well known to both locals and visitors. The signature is the mixed seafood basket with tiger prawns, Andaman mud crab, fish and squid.
items.meta: Beside Chalong pier, Chalong Bay, south of the island

blocks.html: Round things off with the local sweets you can find almost only in Phuket. Many share the same Hokkien-Chinese roots as the savoury dishes, aren't overly sweet, and tend to be good for cooling off.

items: O-aew — shaved ice with jelly made from o-aew seeds and banana, topped with syrup and Chinese herbs. Cool and refreshing; the legendary spot is O-Aew Pao Leng in the Old Town.

Apong — a small fried batter cake that looks like a little pancake, crisp at the edges and soft in the middle, made from flour, sugar, egg and coconut milk. Mae Sunee's apong has earned a Michelin nod.
Tao sor — a thin, layered pastry with both sweet and savoury fillings, a Phuket souvenir with Hokkien-Chinese roots. You'll find it at the souvenir shops around the Old Town.

faq.q: What food should you try in Phuket?
faq.a: Top of the list is Hokkien mee (yellow noodles stir-fried with seafood, Hokkien-Chinese style), moo hong (sweet-savoury braised pork belly), morning dim sum, fiery southern Thai dishes like crab curry with wild betel leaf, and local sweets like o-aew and apong.

faq.q: Where's the best place for Hokkien mee in Phuket?
faq.a: The legend is Mee Ton Poe in the Old Town, open since 1946, and Ko Yoon, which locals rate for its deep, dried-shrimp-fragrant broth. Mee Sapam in Sapam village is the original of Hokkien noodles stir-fried with seafood, done the traditional way.

faq.q: Where do you go for fresh, affordable seafood in Phuket?
faq.a: The Rawai Seafood Market on the south of the island lets you pick fresh seafood by weight and hire a shop to cook it — better value than the tourist beach zones. For a sit-down meal, Laem Hin Seafood and Kan Eang @ Pier are pier-view spots with fresh seafood at reasonable prices.

faq.q: What time does dim sum open in Phuket?
faq.a: Many of the old-school dim sum shops open very early — Boonrat Dim Sum, for instance, opens around 6:00–10:00 and often sells out before mid-morning. For the real local atmosphere, go early and bring cash.

The signature ones are o-aew (shaved ice with Chinese-herb jelly), apong (fried batter cakes, crisp at the edges and soft in the middle), and tao sor (layered pastry with sweet-and-savoury fillings). You'll find them around Phuket's Old Town.
